newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MP demands changes to consumer credit plans.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MP demands changes to consumer credit plans.

text.p: European Commission plans to give consumers greater protection against abusive credit terms are generally good but need amending, according to the European Parliament's rapporteur.

Euro-MP Marlies Mosiek-Urbahn told Reuters she agreed with the main aim of draft directive COM(96)0076, which will impose throughout the European Union a uniform method (the AIBD) for calculating the annual percentage rate of charge for credit (APR).
The main effect will be to force Germany, France and Finland to fall into line with the practice already adopted by the other member states.

But German Christian Democrat said that while the proposal was an improvement on an existing consumer credit directive, 90/88/EEC, and would particularly benefit customers in border areas, the Commission's ideas for calculating the AIBD were flawed.
The Commission recommends the AIBD be set according to a "same-day calculation", whereby the period of a loan is calculated from the first to the last day.

Mosiek Urbahn argued a same-day calculation would have a drawback for customers because the level of the APR would depend on the date on which the loan was paid out and could alter from one month to the next, according to the number of days in the month.
Thus an offer made by a credit institution in January, which has 31 days, would be more favourable than a rival offer drawn up in February, which has two or three days fewer.
Instead the rapporteur recommended a standardised calculation, based on the subdivision of a year into equal intervals.
She said she expected the European Parliament to accept this amendment when it gives the draft directive a first reading (co- decision procedure) next Thursday.

Euro-MPs are also expected to reject the Commission's plan to introduce an identical symbol -- a percentage sign surrounded by the 12 EU stars -- indicating that the uniform AIBD is being used to calculate the APR.

Although the idea of a symbol would in theory allow customers to directly compare APR rates, Mosiek-Urbahn said this would be misleading at the present time because the member states still worked out APRs in a different way.
"There are so many elements used to define the APR and we only have harmonisation on some points," the rapporteur explained.
"We will have to wait until there is more harmonisation," she said, adding that this would be difficult to achieve in the near future.
Mosiek-Urbahn said she expected the Commission to accept the amendment to the proposed method of calculation but was unsure whether it could agree to scrap the 12 star symbol.
